Title: What Happened When We Ran Out of Cards

Messages.Author: Tom Kassel
Messages.Body:
After the discussion of running out of cards, it was amusing that the
next game we played had two players run out. It was a four player game
with:

Tom (Tremere would-be Princes)
Michael (newbie Settite/Assamite/Brujah)
Dave (Lasombra/Ventrue antitribu - showing off his newly acquired
Sabbat - the first seen in our group)
Andrew (Malkavian/Tremere)

When Dave and Andrew got voting vamps into play before my first prince
or Praxis Seizure opportunity, I knew it would be a grim night.
Although Dave was making a mess of Andrew with stealthy bleed, I
couldn't persuade Andrew of the need for a voting block against Dave
and discarded Seizures furiously until Michael took an opportunity to
card flow a vote reaction in my favor making Muaziz my only Prince of
the game.

Michael switched the seating making himself Andrew's prey, which worked
nicely for me as Dave soon ousted Andrew and then Michael. By this
time we each had 5-6 vamps in play, with blood dolls and hunting
grounds to stabilize pool. I was running low on cards, but my final
hand had three 2nd Trad (? - the untap and +2 intercept anyway) which
was enough to see off his final stealthy attempts and drain his library
and hand as well. Muaziz and her friend whose name I forget who also
had inherent stealth then bled Dave into the ground. A pleasing 2-2
draw after a grim start. Andrew sneered "Draw, hmmph" but I replied
"Not for you it wasn't".

So I quickly join the consensus that the Sabbat withdrawal rule sucks.

Tom

Sent via Deja.com http://www.deja.com/
Before you buy.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 28 Jul 2000 09:16:41 GMT, Tom Kassel wrote:

>After the discussion of running out of cards, it was amusing that the
>next game we played had two players run out. It was a four player game
>with:

>....

>So I quickly join the consensus that the Sabbat withdrawal rule sucks.

The way things went, you were able to turn a small difference in final
stength between you and Dave into 2 VP for ousting him and surviving.
If he had been able to withdraw after he ran out of cards then the
final score would have been 2-1 to him, instead of the 2-2 draw. This
would have been a fairer result and a more satisfactory one. As it
was, the conclusion to the game was a hurriedly abbreviated affair as
you and Dave didn't want to keep me and Michael waiting. On the
evidence of this game, the original withdrawal rule does indeed blow
chunks and Sabbat withdrawal is better. I'm bringing my Sabbat rules
sheet along next time - we didn't get the Sabbat voting rules right
either.

Andrew

Which certainly doesn't happen at all with experienced players. The
early-ousted are often able to get a five-player pickup game in while
a tournament round is finishing, and finish BEFORE the round does!

The game is long not because of "long range strategies", but because
of its depth and complexity. This leads to a much better game,
although it does have a slight downside. Players who "turtle", or
begin "going right", or any of a number of phrases for an obnoxious
strategy, generally are going to lose in the end anyway, BECAUSE of
that permanent-force buildup.

DungeonQuest (a board game), on the other hand, was the extreme
opposite. You stepped into the dungeon, drew up your tile, it was a
bottomless pit. Roll to see if you avoid it- nope, you die. Your
opponent wins. That was fun! Want to play again?

In actuality, DungeonQuest was terribly fun. The gameplay was largely
random and required minimal, if any, strategic thought. But the games
also took ten to fifteen minutes, tops. It's a situation where you
pick what you want out of a game, and go there.

Vampire is intended to be a long, drawn out game, representing the
centuries of planning and manipulation of a Methuselah.

The little I have played of Shadowfist suggests that it was intended to
go significantly faster.

If you want a fast, deadly game, V:TES is not the game to play. Its
entire design and strategy allow a game to be slowed down to a snail's
pace, by a Methuselah who wants to, for whatever reason. I once played
a game in Cardiff where 5 people were playing. First person bleeds.
Person two bounces to three. Three bounces to four. Four bounces to
five. Five throws down Second Tradition and blocks, and has
miscellaneous other intercept (both transient and permanent) and bleed
reduction to stop you. The game went slowly.

On Tue, 01 Aug 2000 08:51:33 +0100, Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com>
wrote:

>On Mon, 31 Jul 2000 16:23:53 -0400, Derek Ray wrote:

>>fast bleed and/or vote decks?

>I'm not convinced that it's balanced but, leaving that aside, the
>reason to tilt the balance in favour of fast decks is to speed the
>game up.

It's not necessary to speed the game up. Among experienced players,
it moves PLENTY fast. Inexperienced players will have a learning
curve in ANY game, more so with one this complex. Especially if you,
as most new groups/players do, stop to explain and/or debate things
during the game itself.

>>Why would this have been fairer?
>

>Because Dave ousted two players in their prime. Tom ousted Dave after
>they had both run out of cards and by a narrow margin. Beating one

>person narrowly should not compare with beating two handsomely.

So Dave nuked two weak decks, and Tom was able to oust Dave even
though Dave had gained an additional 12 pool via oustings - and that
12 pool is a LOT! Letting your prey oust anyone is normally a Very
Bad Thing - I routinely use Eagle's Sight in my intercept decks to
save my grandprey from the "killing blow". A deck that is able to
oust 2 players is usually in position, with the extra pool, to
complete the sweep. To overturn that is a sign of a good deck in its
own right.

Also, if I read Tom's message correctly, I have to object as well - it
was NOT a narrow margin, as these things go. It was a concedable
position - when one player has permanent blood gain and permanent
stealth bleed, and the other player does not, it is generally a
horribly bad thing for the other player. Muaziz and Rebecca combined
with a Hunting Ground and Blood Doll definitely qualify as "long term
assets".

The game is balanced this way because of the "seating position" thing.
If you have four strong decks and one weak deck at the table, the
person who is the predator of the weak deck has a free VP, and the
person who is the PREY of the weak deck has a free ride early on.
Once the weak deck is ousted, the stronger predator will run up
against his new stronger prey, and things will begin to return to
balance. The other two players are going to have to settle in for the
longer term and wait until the two players who had an advantage have
beaten each other up a bit.

An early oust means nothing other than deck failure on the part of the
oustee - not necessarily a guarantee of deck strength on the part of
the ouster.

>>Note that there are 4 VPs and 2-1 means that a VP has been "lost"
>>somewhere - increasing the # of draws and timeouts is NOT a good thing.
>
>You've lost me too. The result was a draw. If withdrawal had been
>possible, it would not have been a draw.

Sorry, I abbreviated that too much.

On a 4-player table, there are a total of 4 VPs to be gained. One for
each of the three players ousted, and one for the last man standing.

Withdrawal rules screw this up. A person who withdraws gains no VP
(appropriate), but nobody else gains his VP either. This results in a
net loss of one VP to the table, since as you state the results would
have been 2-1. This is not important UNTIL you are in a tournament,
where total number of VPs determines who reaches the finals. People
running fast run-out-of-cards bleed decks become almost untouchable,
as they oust two people and then leave their table, guaranteeing that
nobody else at that table can surpass them. 2 VPs per round will, in
most tourneys, guarantee you a seat in the finals.

Timeouts do this as well, to some degree.

Normal withdrawal is almost impossible to succeed with, and that is
fine with everyone. Sabbat withdrawal would be very easy to manage in
a deck designed for it - Deal with the Devil being an excellent card
for the purpose, especially up next to a Rumors of Gehenna or
Parthenon.

>>No, sorry. Sabbat withdrawal honks like a big dog, and encourages
>>stupid play since if you can run out of cards in a losing position
>>before you're ousted, you survive. That's absolutely not what was
>>intended, nor is it appropriate.
>
>One supposes that it was what the Sabbat designers intended.

One may suppose that all he wants. The original Jyhad design,
however, is what we opt to be faithful to, not the overpowered
standalone expansion. =)

>Appropriateness is in the eye of the beholder.

Then behold the Deal with the Devil example above and keep telling me
how appropriate it is that a deck can deliberately run itself out of
cards to "escape" certain death, as opposed to actually having to
provide for its own defense.

Certainly. Consider that if I run really fast and oust you with a
Govern the Unaligned, Command the Beast (the +1) and Conditioning type
combination in the first few turns, and play Pentex Loves You(tm) for
some more, you haven't had a chance to build up defences. It's an easy
kill.

Later in the game, a Methuselah may have gained loads of pool from Fifth
Tradition/Minion Tap, Consanguineous Boon, Voter Captivation or
whatever. A late kill can be unthinkably difficult.

I remember a very awkward game once, where Mark Baxter was my prey. I
was playing Ventrue lease and loan, along with some bleed. I'd done not
badly pool wise, but was jamming my hand. It became incredibly cut and
thrust and I eventually managed to oust him with a 1 point Day Op. A
hideously tortuous end game, where it could eventually have gone all
down the pan for me.

--

James Coupe

>So it doesn't really matter whether you can withdraw or not - what

>matters is racking up those 2 VPs, right? Fast bleeders look like the
>best way to go regardless - bleeding your prey is the basic objective
>of the game, after all. Anyway, I still fail to see the point you're
>making about draws.

Fast bleed decks are a good way to go, yes. The dangers in playing
one are multiple, however - a deck that can bleed rapidly and take out
multiple Methuselahs has usually had to sacrifice things like combat
defense, and if it sits next to a combat deck, will normally die
horribly with 0VP. Fast bleed decks have been known to oust the table
for their prey when faced with heavy Deflection. And if you play a
strong-appearing deck, you may be hit with a bunch of cross-table
nastiness. So fast bleed decks don't really dominate the scene at
all.

Slight clarification: reducing your prey's pool is the basic
objective of the game. Bleed is merely one fashion to do it, although
it is surprising to see someone go through a game without bleeding
occasionally.

The point about draws was more that if you start arbitrarily
permitting the removal of VPs from a table (by, say, Sabbat
withdrawal), you hurt the other people at that table's chances at
minimal cost to yourself. It was mostly another nail I was applying
to Sabbat withdrawal's coffin.

>My preference would be for the game to provide a means of making a
>fighting withdrawal - something between the automatic withdrawal of
>Sabbat and the impossible withdrawal of Jyhad. E.g. allow a player to
>declare that he is withdrawing and then for him to do so if he hasn't
>been bled by the start of his next turn. This would be a reasonable
>effect for a new Master or Vote card (assuming that one doesn't
>already exist).

I think it would need to be a bit more difficult than that, as it's
possible to make it very hard for your predator to bleed you. Perhaps
trim down the Jyhad rules a bit (i haven't looked at that particular
rule in forever, mostly because i know it won't ever fly), and see
what comes out. But the Sabbat withdrawal rule is just plain silly.

I don't think Jyhad takes an inordinate number of
turns to finish a game compared to other CCGs.
In a tournament it's probably a rare game that
goes more than twelve times around the table.
That would be sixty player-turns at most. In
Magic, a game where both players get 30 turns
would be long but not unheard of. In Shadowfist
it might be more unusual (in a 4-player game,
that would be 15 turns per player), but Fist is
definitely a faster-paced game than Jyhad.

To me, at least, the slow progress of Jyhad games
is part of the flavor of the game. And I think it's
due largely to each player having typically at least
three or four minions, all of whom you have to make
decisions for, and who may end up playing several
cards each every turn.

> What does seem take longer than other CCG is reading the card texts -
> even allowing for my unfamiliarity, they seem particularly wordy and
> opaque. More use of symbols instead of words for the disciplines and
> clans (as in Sabbat) might help.

Well, in my group, people hardly ever read the card
texts. Because we know most of the cards by heart...
Obviously this isn't so much the case for people still
learning the game, but eventually I think you'll see
much less text-reading slowing you down. What slows
*us* down is (no really!) people thinking about things
during their turns. Some people more than others...
but that tends to be true of any game.

Josh

withdrawal very difficult to do. The Sabbat rule takes this to the

gives an advantage to some decks, while giving other decks a
disadvantage. I agree that the Sabbat rule doesn't make a build-up
style deck impossible, but it does (as Richard said) have a deleterious
effect on that style.

Messages.Author: Chris Shorb
Messages.Body:
I believe that the Sabbat Withdrawal rules were brought into play along
with cards like Raptor and Dirty Little Secrets to encourage "Millstone"
type decks a la M:TG. It also was to encourage a 4th method of prey
destruction (besides bleed, vote, and combat) which not coincidentally
would aid the Nosferatu and Nos!, who really don't *excel* at any of the
other 3 (except maybe pot combat [PDB6 et.al]). Please don't post your
decks that prove that Nos(!) can be really good at those three. I think
a good Ventrue vote deck played by an excellent player will always do
better than a good Nos vote deck played by same excellent player, all
other factors being identical (which never happens, but we're talking
theory here). And the same for bleed.

I think there is still room for it, but I think that it would actually
help if the rule gave the withdrawer's predator a VP (but say, not the 6
pool). I don't think it will encourage faster decks, since a speed
bleed deck or a speed vote deck will oust a prey or three long before
the prey has run out of cards. It might actually encourage the use of
more permanents, since by their very nature, a permanent does not use up
as much card resource (Tasha Morgan vs Threats at minor - which uses up
more card resource per action?). Of course, then a Feldon's Cane type
card would have to be introduced (take your entire ash heap and
reshuffle it into your library), which brings us closer to Magic - and
we all know how Anathema that can be...

I haven't thought this through really, so I welcome all your comments to
point out the glaring holes in my logic...

Chris

Why is disengaging so critical to a "hit and run" deck? In fact,
disengaging (by Sabbat rules) only allows you to deny the VP someone would
have gotten for you being ousted after running through your deck. It
doesn't gain the player himself anything directly. This also allows another
avenue to a king-maker strategy(oust someone, then deny another by
cancelling your own VP? No thanks...) Varying the number of VP per table
by such an easy means can't be good for tournament play, either.

>The
>Sabbat withdrawal rules don't make a long-haul deck impossible. They
>just reduce the opportunity to score VP and you stil1 get 1 VP for
>surviving.
>

1 VP on a five player table represents 20% of all available VP. On a four
player table, its 25%. Imagine reducing a player's opportunity to score
that much in _any_ other game, and you can see how poor an idea it is.
